transcript:
[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Jordan Lee from Redwood. Quick intro - Samira is our SE and Diego's on for any deep infra questions.
[00:12] Alex: Hi, Alex here, thanks. We want to see the hosted API for chat features, mainly streaming and how to control costs.
[00:20] Jordan: Perfect. Agenda - quick overview of Redwood API, demo chat generation with streaming, how params affect output and cost, retry and backoff behavior, and time for questions.
[00:35] Samira: I'll jump into the demo - open the Redwood Console and a sample node/python snippet - bear with me if there's a little screen lag.
[00:50] Diego: note, the console demo will show the per-token cost and latency breakdown - helps product teams.
[01:10] [screen share] Samira: Alright, here's a chat request. A couple important fields: messages (role/content), model selection, temperature, top_p, max_tokens, and stream=true for chunked responses.
[01:35] Marcus: How does streaming work if a message is long? Do we get partial tokens?
[01:42] Samira: Yes - with stream=true you get incremental chunks as the model generates. Useful for UI snappyness. The SDK exposes an event stream and we also provide server-sent events and websockets in some SDKs.
[02:05] Alex: Any gotchas around reassembly or ordering? We've seen out-of-order chunks with other vendors.
[02:13] Samira: Good question. Redwood's stream is ordered; each chunk has an index and partial delta. However transcript-level glitches can happen if client retries mid-stream, so we recommend deterministic request ids for idempotency.
[02:40] [00:03:00] Samira: Let's talk params - temperature controls randomness: 0 is deterministic, 0.7 is common for creative responses. top_p does nucleus sampling; use one or the other typically. max_tokens caps output length which directly impacts cost.
[03:10] Priya: For our use case we want short, factual responses and sometimes longer step-by-step outputs. What's best practice?
[03:18] Samira: For factual short answers set temperature 0-0.2, max_tokens 150-250. For longer step-by-step, bump max_tokens and maybe temperature 0.2-0.4. Also use stop sequences to avoid runaway tokens.
[03:42] Jordan: On cost, remember tokens in prompt + output both count. Redwood Console shows token burn per route so you can see which prompts drive cost.
[04:00] Marcus: Do you support system messages and tool calls?
[04:05] Samira: Yes - system, user, assistant roles. We also support function/tool calling patterns; and structured outputs via JSON schema enforcement.
[04:20] [00:05:10] Samira: Retry behavior - Redwood client implements exponential backoff + jitter for transient 5xx and 429s. We also expose retry hooks so you can customize. Important: make requests idempotent where possible; include a client_request_id.
[04:45] Alex: If we re-send after a timeout, will the model produce duplicate content?
[04:52] Samira: Potentially. We recommend one of two strategies: use short-lived server-side caches keyed by client_request_id to dedupe; or have the client stream to an append-only buffer and reconcile. For most hosted customers the built-in retry/backoff is sufficient.
[05:15] Diego: On throttling: we have rate limits per API key/route - console shows quota and current usage. For production we'll recommend burst policies or move to Dedicated if sustained high throughput is required.
[05:40] Priya: Security - can you walk us through data retention and encryption?
[05:45] Samira: Sure. Hosted API by default retains only minimal logs for SRE and debugging, customers can request reduced retention. We support TLS-in-transit, envelope encryption at rest, and KMS integrations for key control. We have SOC2 Type II and can share the report.
[06:10] Marcus: Do you support SSO for the console and RBAC?
[06:15] Jordan: Yes, SSO/SAML, SCIM provisioning, and role-based access controls. We'll share the security pack after the call.
[06:30] [00:07:00] Samira: Demo - I'll send three requests in quick succession. Watch the streaming behavior: first chunk at ~200ms, subsequent chunks as tokens generated.
[07:00] [sound of typing] Samira: First response streamed fine. Second request we intentionally set high temperature to show variability.
[07:30] Marcus: Looks good. Can you show partial response cancellation? If the user hits stop in the UI, can we halt generation and still use partial token content?
[07:40] Samira: Yes, client can close stream; the server will stop generation and return partial output. The SDK surfaces partial content and a truncated flag.
[08:00] Alex: How about latency metrics - p50/p95?
[08:06] Diego: We publish p50/p95 per model under typical payload sizes; console includes per-route latency histograms. For low-latency needs we recommend smaller context windows, lower batch sizes, and streaming to improve perceived latency.
[08:30] Priya: If we need guaranteed tail latency, is Dedicated the only option?
[08:36] Jordan: Dedicated gives predictable throughput and lower tail latency because you get reserved GPUs. For many teams, hosted SLOs suffice. We can discuss SLAs in contracts.
[08:55] [00:09:15] Samira: A quick note on batching and KV cache - for chat with long context we optimize KV cache to avoid recomputing past tokens; batching helps throughput at slight latency cost. Redwood Optimize has recommendations for batching/quantization per workload.
[09:20] Marcus: Interested in the Optimize tooling - can it suggest quantization profiles for our fine-tuned flows?
[09:28] Samira: Yes, Optimize analyzes request shapes and suggests model variants and quantization to reduce cost while maintaining quality; it's more relevant for Dedicated/Private but we use it to guide hosted suggestions too.
[09:50] Alex: Any limitations for PII or regulated data? We process health data in some flows.
[09:58] Jordan: For PHI/PII, we recommend Private or Dedicated with our Private control plane and KMS. Hosted can be used with contractual data handling terms but for regulated PHI many customers choose Private. We'll include compliance notes in the security pack.
[10:25] [00:11:00] Samira: Walkthrough of retry headers - the API returns x-retry-after, request-id and streaming-chunk-index headers. Use request-id for tracing across retries.
[10:45] Marcus: For long-running generations, should we use websockets?
[10:50] Samira: Websockets are recommended for very low-latency interactivity; SSE works fine for most web UIs.
[11:10] Priya: About pricing - can we get a ballpark for our estimated 100k monthly tokens?
[11:16] Jordan: I'll send a pricing sheet - rough math in console shows estimated monthly cost under current usage; we'll tailor discounts for pilot.
[11:35] Alex: Great. One more - model upgrades and versioning: how do you handle breaking changes?
[11:40] Samira: You can pin model versions in routes and do canary rollouts. If a model update is incompatible we notify customers and provide opt-in. Rollouts support A/B and automatic fallback to previous variant.
[12:05] [00:12:30] Jordan: Alright let's recap next steps - we'll send quickstart, security docs, trial creds, and schedule a POC scoping call. Anything else?
[12:20] Priya: We'd like a short checklist for integration steps and a sample prompt set for benchmarking.
[12:25] Marcus: I'll assemble traffic profile and sample prompts.
[12:30] Jordan: Perfect. Thanks everyone - we'll follow up via email and add items to the CRM.
[12:40] Alex: Thanks Jordan, Samira.
[12:44] [call ends]
notes: Customer leaning toward hosted pilot but flagged data residency + PHI as gating factors. Redwood SE recommended Private for regulated workloads and Dedicated for predictable low tail latency. POC to focus on sample prompts, token burn analysis, and streaming UX. Security pack requested.
